meta.description: Not Eban's line. The oldest record is 1922: Shaw is credited with calling Lord Rosebery a man who never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Some People Never Miss an Opportunity to Miss an Opportunity'?
meta.ogDescription: Abba Eban popularized it from 1970 — but the jibe is documented in 1922, credited to Bernard Shaw about Lord Rosebery. The full chronology.

answer.label: Not Abba Eban — credited to George Bernard Shaw
answer.authorDates: 1856–1950 · Irish-born playwright and critic · credited at second hand, in 1922
answer.sourceLine: The oldest documented form is not Eban’s. It sits on page 35 of Private Diaries of the Rt. Hon. Sir Algernon West, G.C.B. (E. P. Dutton, 1922), where West recalls that “Bernard Shaw, in later years, described him as a man who never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity” — “him” being Lord Rosebery. Abba Eban used his own versions of the joke from October 1970 onward and made it a diplomatic catchphrase, but he did not coin it; equally, Quote Investigator ↗ has found no Shaw writing or transcribed speech that contains it, so the 1922 credit is itself hearsay.

source.heading: The earliest documented version

docMeta.dd: Private Diaries of the Rt. Hon. Sir Algernon West, G.C.B.
E. P. Dutton, New York, 1922 — page 35
West’s recollection of a remark by Bernard Shaw about Lord Rosebery; no date or occasion given

source.excerpt: He was a man well described by my friend Lord Welby as one who was always craving for sympathy and never knew how to get it. Bernard Shaw, in later years, described him as a man who never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity, and W. Johnson, afterwards Cory the Eton master, said in a classical allusion that he wanted the palm without the dust.
trail: 1922 — The jibe first appears in print in Sir Algernon West’s posthumously published diaries ↗, credited to Bernard Shaw and aimed at Lord Rosebery. The New York Times singled it out when it reviewed the book that October.

1959–1963 — The remark keeps its Rosebery target but loses its exact shape: History Today reprints the 1922 wording in 1959, while Robert Rhodes James’s 1963 biography and The Spectator that March both give it as “never missed a chance of missing an opportunity,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

1970–1972 — Abba Eban makes it his own. At the National Press Club in October 1970 he says “some politicians never lose a chance of missing an opportunity”; he turns it on the United Nations in December 1971; and Robert St. John’s 1972 biography Eban records “there are political leaders who never lose a chance to miss an opportunity” — all documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

1988 onward — The New York Times reports a PLO version as a paraphrase of Eban’s “famous quip,” and the line detaches from everyone. Wikiquote ↗ carries the “Arabs” form on a single 2002 newspaper citation and notes it is often misquoted with “Palestinians.”
source.excerptNote: “He” is Lord Rosebery; the passage comes from West’s account of a stay at Dalmeny during the 1892 general election. Note that the wording is never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity — the neat modern form is a later polish, not what the 1922 page says.

source.useLine: Free to use — but only the 1922 wording quoted here, which is public domain and needs no permission or licence, in commercial and paid presentations included. The tidy modern form (“some people never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity”) has no identified author and no known first publication, so no rights claim can honestly be made about it in either direction.

Dutton in New York in 1922 — comfortably before 1931, so it is in the public domain in the United States and the full volume is free to read at the Internet Archive. That status covers the 1922 wording only: the tidy modern form of the saying has no identified author or first publication, so no rights claim can honestly be made about it.

author.name: George Bernard Shaw
author.heading: Who Shaw was
author.metaLine: 1856–1950 · Irish-born playwright, critic and Fabian polemicist · Nobel Prize in Literature, 1925
author.bio: George Bernard Shaw was the most quotable British public figure of his generation — a playwright, music and drama critic, and Fabian socialist agitator whose stage epigrams and platform one-liners were reprinted, paraphrased and improved upon for half a century. He is the earliest name attached to this jibe, in the 1922 diaries of the Liberal civil servant Sir Algernon West, who recalled Shaw using it about Lord Rosebery. That credit is second-hand: West gives no date and no occasion, and no Shaw text has ever been produced to confirm it — which is exactly the loose, unverifiable way most of the sayings pinned to Shaw came to be pinned to him.

copyAttribution: "Some people never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity" — commonly credited to Abba Eban, but the oldest documented form is in Sir Algernon West's Private Diaries (E. P. Dutton, 1922, p. 35), where Bernard Shaw is said to have described Lord Rosebery as "a man who never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity." Eban used his own versions of the joke from October 1970 onward. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most confidently misattributed one-liners in political speech — and unusually, every name on it is shaky, including the earliest one.

items.why: Eban is the reason anyone knows the joke, but he was born in 1915 and his earliest documented use is a National Press Club speech in October 1970 — where he said “some politicians never lose a chance of missing an opportunity.” The jibe was already in print in 1922. Quote Investigator ↗ calls him “a locus for the remark’s popularization,” not its source.

items.who: “The Arabs never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity”
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ carries this form with a single citation — a Jerusalem Post item dated 18 November 2002, the day after Eban died — and ties it to the Geneva peace conference of 21 December 1973. That is a retrospective note thirty years after the alleged occasion, and three years after Eban’s first documented use of the joke.

Wikiquote records that the “Arabs” version is “often misquoted” with “Palestinians” substituted. Quote Investigator notes that when The New York Times used a PLO version in December 1988 it presented it explicitly as a paraphrase of Eban’s quip, not as his words.

Shaw is named by Sir Algernon West, who gives no date and no occasion for the remark and died in 1921, the year before his diaries were published. Quote Investigator states plainly that it “has not yet located any direct evidence in his writings or transcribed speeches.”

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: the oldest documented form of the joke is the 1922 line about Lord Rosebery in Sir Algernon West’s diaries ↗, credited there to Shaw on hearsay. Everything after that — including Eban’s famous version — is a retelling.

context.heading: Why the line stuck to two very different men
lead: Lord Rosebery was the great political disappointment of late-Victorian Britain: brilliant, rich, hesitant, and visibly unhappy in office. He was Foreign Secretary from 1892 to 1894 and Prime Minister for barely fifteen months, from March 1894 to June 1895, and the men around him kept reaching for the same idea in different words. In the very passage that carries the Shaw jibe, Sir Algernon West stacks three of them: Lord Welby’s man “always craving for sympathy and never knew how to get it,” Shaw’s man who never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity, and Cory’s classical dig that he “wanted the palm without the dust.”

Half a century later the same shape of joke found a much larger stage. Abba Eban was Israel’s foreign minister from 1966 to 1974 and, by common consent, the most fluent English speaker in world diplomacy — a man who wrote his own epigrams and reused the good ones. Quote Investigator documents him deploying the line at the National Press Club in October 1970 (“Some politicians never lose a chance of missing an opportunity”), against the United Nations in December 1971, and again in Robert St. John’s 1972 biography. Once a phrase is that useful, the crowd stops caring who said it first.
detailsBody: The documented chain runs: never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity (1922, and repeated verbatim by History Today in 1959) → never missed a chance of missing an opportunity (Robert Rhodes James’s 1963 Rosebery biography, and The Spectator in March 1963) → never lose a chance of missing an opportunity (Eban, 1970) → never missed an opportunity to miss an opportunity (The New York Times, December 1988, explicitly describing it as a paraphrase of Eban).

No single speaker is on record for the tidy modern form — “some people never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity.” It is what the joke settled into after sixty-odd years of retelling, which is why it can be quoted confidently and sourced to nobody.
context.pull: Rosebery was the original target; Eban was the megaphone.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly credited to Abba Eban, who popularized it from October 1970. The oldest documented form is a 1922 diary entry crediting Bernard Shaw at second hand, about Lord Rosebery; no Shaw writing or transcribed speech confirms it, so no author is established.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest evidence is the 1922 publication of Sir Algernon West's diaries, crediting Bernard Shaw with calling Lord Rosebery a man who "never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity"; it also documents History Today (1959), Robert Rhodes James's Rosebery biography and The Spectator (March 1963) with "never missed a chance of missing an opportunity"; Eban at the National Press Club (Baltimore Sun, 13 Oct 1970) with "some politicians never lose a chance of missing an opportunity"; Eban on the UN (Christian Science Monitor, 29 Dec 1971); Robert St. John's 1972 biography "Eban" p.491; and a New York Times piece of 18 Dec 1988 presenting the PLO version as a paraphrase of Eban's quip. QI concludes it has located no direct evidence in Shaw's writings or transcribed speeches and that Eban is the modern popularizer.

The Internet Archive item is 'Private diaries of the Rt. Hon. Sir Algernon West', by Sir Algernon West (1832-1921), edited by Horace G. Hutchinson, published New York: E. P. Dutton, 1922, with full text freely readable and downloadable.

The full text of the 1922 edition contains, on page 35 (between the running heads 'AT DALMENY 35' and '36 THE GENERAL ELECTION'), the passage: 'He was a man well described by my friend Lord Welby as one who was always craving for sympathy and never knew how to get it. Bernard Shaw, in later years, described him as a man who never missed an occasion of losing an opportunity, and W. Johnson, afterwards Cory the Eton master, said in a classical allusion that he wanted the palm without the dust.'

Wikiquote's Abba Eban page lists 'The Arabs never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity' in its main Quotes section, cited only to The Jerusalem Post (18 November 2002), notes it is 'often misquoted as "Palestinians never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity"', and ties it to the Geneva Peace Conference of 21 December 1973. The page has no 'Misattributed' or 'Disputed' section.

Wikipedia gives Abba Eban's dates as 2 February 1915 - 17 November 2002, describes him as a South African-born Israeli diplomat and politician, records that he was Israel's Foreign Minister 1966-1974, and states the 'never miss an opportunity to miss an opportunity' remark was made after the Geneva peace talks in December 1973.

Wikipedia gives Lord Rosebery's dates as 7 May 1847 - 21 May 1929, Prime Minister 5 March 1894 - 22 June 1895, and Foreign Secretary 18 August 1892 - 10 March 1894, and describes historians judging him a failure in both offices and losing interest in running the government.

Wikipedia gives George Bernard Shaw's dates as 26 July 1856 - 2 November 1950, describes him as a playwright, critic, polemicist and political activist, and records his Nobel Prize in Literature for 1925.

Wikiquote's George Bernard Shaw page contains no instance of 'losing an opportunity', 'missing an opportunity' or 'Rosebery' - i.e. it does not list this jibe among Shaw's sourced or attributed quotations.
